prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision measurement of time

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a new measurement capability, and this is the kind of progress I think physics depends on. Katori's magic-wavelength idea cancels the light shift of the clock transition by design, so thousands of atoms can be interrogated at once without Doppler or recoil broadening. Ye's group then showed that the coherence, linewidth and systematic-control work could be pushed to the 1e-18 fractional-uncertainty level, and tied it to comb and ultrastable-laser technology. That is not a proposal waiting for confirmation. JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and others have reproduced and compared these clocks repeatedly, and the results are used: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on variation of constants, dark-matter searches, relativistic geodesy and the pending redefinition of the second. Seven of eight opening ballots rank it in the top five, and the attribution to two laureates is cleaner than for almost any other shortlisted candidate. The 2005 prize covered the comb and the 2012 prize covered ion control and cavity QED, so this achievement is distinct from both.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is whether the committee will see a clock as an instrument milestone rather than a discovery, and whether it is a separate achievement from combs (2005) and ion clocks (2012). There is also an attribution risk. Ion-clock groups (Al+ at NIST, Yb+ at PTB), the Paris/SYRTE lattice-clock work and the early Sr clock groups also contributed to the field, and two names will leave some of them out. Finally, the headline impact, the redefinition of the second, has not yet happened. I rely on my own recollection of the credit history and have not verified priority details.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B007 first as an instrument-level discovery that nature and experiment confirm, with clean attribution to Katori and Ye, and mature after two decades of replication.
responses.response: I agree on the ranking and on the maturity. I would add that the replication comes from comparisons between independent clocks, not only from reproducing a number. That is stronger evidence than most candidates have. I would qualify one point. Danielsson mentions Lemonde and Ludlow as possible additions. I think the Katori and Ye attribution holds, because the magic-wavelength concept and the record-accuracy realisation are separable, identifiable steps. The ion-clock community was largely covered by 2012, so I would not reopen the credit. Danielsson also ranks B001 second and calls the recognition slightly early. I agree, but on B001 I would go further than he does, because the superconducting pairing remains unresolved.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B058) first because it underpins superconducting processors, and ranks B007 second as a timely precision-measurement advance, while noting that the 2025 prize on circuits may make B058 feel too close.
responses.response: I take the point that circuit QED is foundational, and I do not dismiss it. But the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits makes a second award from the same platform harder to defend this year. Johansson himself notes that Wallraff's experimental role is not in the credited names, so the allocation is not settled. B007 has no such overlap and no open credit gap. I would not call it a technology prize against Johansson's concern for B058, since the clocks are used to measure, as a result of their performance, not only as hardware. My view is that B058 is a good candidate for a later year, and that this year B007 is the stronger and cleaner case.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B007 first, stressing that the light shift is cancelled by design and that atomic theory and experiment agree to extraordinary precision, and ranks B015 (Cirac and Zoller) second.
responses.response: I agree with her on B007 and value her atomic-structure perspective on the magic-wavelength condition and the blackbody shift, which is where the systematics for lattice clocks are hard. On B015 I respectfully differ in ranking. The Cirac-Zoller gate proposal is original, but the experimental realisation was done by Wineland, Blatt, Monroe and others, so a theory-only prize now would be separated from the experimental credit, and the 2022 and 2025 prizes have recently covered adjacent quantum-information ground. I would keep B015 off my list of alternatives for this reason, though it would be a legitimate prize in a different year.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene (B001) first for its direct theory-experiment loop and large field impact, and places B007 only fifth.
responses.response: I accept that the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 experiments is a striking sequence and that many groups have reproduced the correlated phases, so I rank B001 as my first alternative. My reservations are about maturity and credit. The superconducting pairing mechanism is still debated, which Eriksson concedes, and the experimental credit is awkward: Yuan Cao and the other first authors, and the contemporaneous work of other groups, are outside the three names. I want the quantity measured stably before honouring it, and the lattice clocks have had two more decades to be tested by independent comparisons. I am open to being persuaded, but I do not see B001 as obviously ahead of B007 on maturity or on the cleanliness of attribution.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the IceCube neutrino discovery (B039) first as a purpose-built detector opening a new observational window, and ranks B007 second.
responses.response: I like the instrument-driven logic, and a new window on the universe is just the type of opening I value. My concern is attribution. IceCube is a collaboration of several hundred people, the AMANDA and DUMAND precursors complicate priority, and Olsson also said she cannot identify who made the decisive analysis steps. With Halzen, Karle and Spiering, the prize would be a judgment of leadership rather than of a specific demonstrated step. Source identification is only partly independent so far, since KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD are still maturing. For B007 the contributions are traceable to two people. I would keep B039 out of my alternatives for now.

uncertainties: Whether colleagues treat the lattice clock as an invention of a new measurement method rather than a technology milestone.
Whether two names are enough, or whether the committee will want to credit Lemonde, Ludlow or the ion-clock groups, and whether the credit history I recall is accurate.
Whether a prize before the redefinition of the second is timely or slightly early.
If the committee prefers two achievements, B007 leaves only one name for a second part, so B007 pairs naturally only with a single-laureate part, which none of the shortlisted candidates offers.
statement.conflict_note: My profile shows a possible connection. I spent a year of my PhD in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Hall was Jun Ye's mentor at JILA, so I have a personal link to the group environment of one proposed laureate. I also work in Lund atomic physics and in quantum memories, which is adjacent to the cold-atom and quantum-information candidates (B008, B015, B005). My work did not involve Ye or Katori directly, so I see no formal conflict, but I flag the connection to the chair and will recuse if the committee judges it necessary.
